paper_title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards, with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Lean4AgenticRL**, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. **Lean4AgenticRL** first builds a *problem-specific workflow* system that balances the agent's own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using **Lean4AgenticRL**, we train **LAR-9B/27B**, a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of similar size. **LAR-27B** achieves **77.3%** on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by **9.89%** and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by **5.07%**. These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform long-running agentic tasks has been regarded as key capability by the computer science community (Wang et al., 2026b). This capability is typically evaluated by solving complex software engineering (SWE) (Jimenez et al., 2024) and terminal-usage (Team, 2025c) tasks within advanced harness frameworks (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2025; Merrill & Shaw, 2025). Given the significant practical value (OpenAI, 2026), training advanced agentic LLMs has become an important research direction. Agentic capability in LLMs refers to the models ability to actively interact with an environment to explore, understand, and resolve tasks. Previous works have developed multiple approaches to strengthen this ability, including simple prompting (Yao et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023) and building supervised fine-tuning datasets (Pan et al., 2024; Badertdinov et al., 2026). Building on the success of scaling Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (Guo et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025) and multi-turn agentic RL methods (Pan et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c), the community has driven significant progress in long-horizon agent tasks such as SWE and terminal-usage. Despite significant progress in large-scale agentic RL, reliably assigning process rewards in long agent traces remains an open problem. In particular, current agentic RL methods (Zeng et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026) primarily rely on high-level outcome rewards, building on their success in single-turn RLVR. This has motivated the use of process rewards to supervise the agents intermediate steps (Wang et al., 2026c; Xi et al., 2026). However, existing approaches often focus on low-level toolcall results, which may overlook broader workflow progress and degrade performance when single toolcall cannot directly connect to the task objectives (Modecrua et al., 2026). Overall, these limitations highlight the need to unify the high-level outcome rewards, mid-level workflowstage rewards, and low-level toolcall rewards in verifiable way to enable more effective agentic RL. To address the above limitations, we propose Lean4AgenticRL, unified framework for deriving multi-level rewards within uniform, Lean4Agent verifiable, open-ended agentic RL setting. The overview of Lean4AgenticRL is presented in Figure 1. In Lean4AgenticRL, we first use problemspecific workflow (PSWF) agent system that balances the agents inherent capabilities with execution controls through plan-then-execute paradigm. It further provides the basis for verifying agent behaviors. Subsequently, we extend the Lean4Agent (Wang et al., 2026b) verification framework from fixed workflows to general harnesses. Then, we formalize the PSWF and segment the agent trajectories into formal workflow stages and annotate the trajectories with high-level outcome rewards (α), mid-level workflow-stage rewards (β), and low-level toolcall rewards (γ). These reward signals synergistically support learning from both final outcomes and intermediate behaviors through our workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm, enabling more effective agentic RL. We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We propose Lean4AgenticRL, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards within Lean, uniform dependent-type verifiable language, for agentic RL in open-ended domains that enables more effective agentic RL. (2) We develop problem-specific workflow and generalize the current agent verification framework from fixed workflow to general harness systems. They greatly enlarge the applicability of the current uniform formal agent verification system. (3) We train LAR-9B/27B

sections.title: 2 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: We detail the formulation of the Lean4AgenticRL framework in this section. The goal of Lean4AgenticRL is to derive multi-level rewards in uniform Lean schema to achieve more effective agentic RL in open-ended domains. Section 2.1 introduces the key preliminaries, Section 2.2 details the formulation of Problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system, Section 2.3 introduces the workflow formalization and reward annotation method, and Section 2.4 shows how we train the model using the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO method.

sections.title: 2.2 PROBLEM-SPECIFIC WORKFLOW AGENT SYSTEM
sections.content: This section introduces the problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system. It aims to balance the controllability of fixed-workflow execution against the flexibility of free-form, ReAct-style execution. It also lays the foundation for our further verification process. In particular, we achieve this by plan-then-execute paradigm.

sections.title: 2.3.3 TOOLCALL LOW-LEVEL REWARD ANNOTATION
sections.content: Since part of the predicate judgment in β rewards relies on LLM-as-judge verification, the policy may learn to hack the reward through ritualistic behaviors rather than resolving the task. For example, to satisfy the predicate that requires repeated fix-and-retry attempts, the agent can simply rerun the same testing bash command several times and thereby mislead the judge. To address this issue, we further extend the formal predicate system from the workflow level to finer-grained toolcall level. Specifically, we implement set of symbolic predicates, including consecutive repetition, noop commands, const shell, , and evaluate them using Lean and Python checkers to target these common reward-hacking patterns. The full list of penalized behaviors is presented in Appendix I.2. With this annotation, each step τi receives low-level toolcall reward γi {1, 0}. Here, we deliberately set γ to penalty-only reward that punishes violations of the step without granting any positive reward, so the policy cannot exploit γ itself to overwhelm other positive rewards. Consequently, we obtain symbolic guard that largely prevents most commonly observed reward-hacking strategies against β.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENT
sections.content: We validate the effectiveness of Lean4AgenticRL and the performance of LAR-9B/27B model based on SWE-Bench-Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024), TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 (Team, 2025c). Specifically, we present the main results in Section 3.3 and compare the training dynamics with outcome-reward GRPO in Section 3.4. Subsequently, we conduct ablation studies in Section 3.5 and case study in Section 3.6. We also perform additional experiments in Appendix D.

sections.title: 3.1.1 TASK AND BENCHMARK
sections.content: We assess the LAR models in two advanced agentic tasks, namely, software engineering (SWE) and general terminal usage. They are measured by SWE-Bench-Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 (Team, 2025c), both of which are widely adopted in evaluating frontier LLMs (Qwen Team, 2026a; Zeng et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026; Anthropic, 2026c; Xu et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026). We evaluate on SWE-Bench-Verified under mean@3, and on TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 under mean@5, using randomized seeds. Further details on the benchmarks and tasks are presented in Appendix G.

sections.title: 3.1.2 BASELINES
sections.content: To evaluate the effectiveness of the Lean4AgenticRL and the LAR-9B/27B models, we compare them with the latest open-weight models of similar size. Following previous works (Ivison et al., 2026; Qwen Team, 2026a), for the 9B model, we mainly compared with OpenThinkerAgent-V1 (Team, 2025a), Qwen-3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), TMax-9B (Ivison et al., 2026), and Gemma-4-12B (Farabet & Lacombe, 2026). The 27B-level model is compared with Qwen-3.627B (Qwen Team, 2026b), TMax-27B (Ivison et al., 2026), Qwen-3-Coder-30B (Team, 2025b) Gemma-4-31B (Farabet & Lacombe, 2026), and Qwen-3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026c). All the baselines run with the highest reasoning effort and the longest supported context length to elicit their best performance. For the agent harness, we report the results on Terminus-2 (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) for TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 and Claude-code (Anthropic, 2026a) for SWE-Bench-Verified. 3.

sections.title: 3.4 COMPARED WITH DIRECT RL TRAINING
sections.content: In this section, we investigate the performance of Lean4AgenticRL compared to normal GRPObased agentic RL using pure outcome rewards under the OpenClaw-RL (Wang et al., 2026c) framework. In particular, we conducted the training with 1616 step size using SWE-ReBench (Badertdinov et al., 2026) for 30 steps on the SWE task, or TMax (Ivison et al., 2026) for 80 steps on the terminal-usage task, both based on Qwen-3.5-9B. Throughout the training, we evaluate the intermediate checkpoint on SWE-Bench-Verified with pass@1 and on TerminalBench-2.0 with mean@3. The training dynamics are presented in Figure 2. The results show that Lean4AgenticRL outperforms the GRPO baseline throughout training on both tasks. On the SWE task, GRPO improves during the first 15 steps but then quickly deteriorates, falling back to roughly its initial level by step 20, while Lean4AgenticRL improves steadily over all 30 steps. We hypothesize that pure outcome rewards may reward some intermediate steps that are not functioning as desired, thereby destabilizing training at later stage. In the terminal usage task, GRPO fluctuates substantially and improves slowly, with pronounced mid-task degradation, whereas Lean4AgenticRL maintains clear upward trend with consistent margin. Moreover, Lean4AgenticRL is more efficient in terms of training steps; it surpasses the best GRPO checkpoint within 10 steps on SWE and 30 steps on terminal-usage. Based on our full training, the performance to increase on both tasks as the training proceeds.

sections.title: 3.5.1 DROPPING PROBLEM-SPECIFIC WORKFLOW
sections.content: We first examine whether the PSWF system itself benefits the agent execution without training. Specifically, we evaluate Qwen-3.5-9B on SWE-Bench-Verified in the Claude-code harness, with or without the PSWF. The results are shown in Table 2, which shows that removing PSWF reduces the resolution rate from 44.0% to 42.4%. When we take closer look at the failed trajectories, we observe that without PSWF guidance, the agent often explores the repository insufficiently, fails to locate the relevant files, and misattributes the root cause of the issue. This experiment demonstrates that, rather than limiting the agents capabilities, applying the PSWF alone can improve the performance of LLM agents.

sections.title: Method
sections.content: SWE-Bench-Verified Table 2: Ablation Studies Result This experiment aims to assess the role of γ by repeating the 30-step SWE training in Section 3.4 with γ removed from the reward, while keeping all other settings unchanged. As shown in Table 2, removing γ reduces the performance of the model by 6.6%. It also increases the number of repeated commands captured by γ by 66.8% compared to the base model, while the full Lean4AgenticRL training observed almost no such behavior. Removing γ also increases the total number of tool calls by 18.7% compared to the full Lean4AgenticRL. Without this guard, the policy quickly learns to hack the LLM-as-judge predicates in β through ritualistic actions, such as echo and repeated read-only or placeholder commands. As the training proceeds, these actions fill the context and inflate the response length with little contribution to the solutions. In contrast, with γ in place, the response length of Lean4AgenticRL grows steadily alongside its performance, and we observed almost no reward hacking activities guarded by γ. sections.title: 4.1 AGENTIC REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
sections.content: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become scalable approach to enhancing LLM capabilities. It was first scaled by OpenAI-O1 (OpenAI, 2024) and open-sourced by DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) and Kimi-K1.5 (Team et al., 2025). RLVR shows that simple verifier-based outcome rewards can elicit reasoning capabilities without learning reward models. Building on this paradigm, agentic RL extends it to multi-turn agent interactions, typically rewarding the correctness of the final answer or task success (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025). However, as the agents task extends over longer horizon, sparse outcome rewards that assign identical credit to every step cannot distinguish useful intermediate actions from redundant or erroneous ones. To provide denser training signals, subsequent studies apply process rewards on individual tool calls or infer step-level rewards from LLM judges (Yu et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Xi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c). However, these signals are largely tied to low-level tool calls, which overlook broader progress and may even impair optimization (Modecrua et al., 2026). Prior work on hierarchical credit assignment (Kazemnejad et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2026) relies on highly similar trajectories or tree-search methods, setting that differs substantially from open-ended tasks such as SWE and general terminal usage. separate line of work replaces LLM judges with symbolic or algorithmic oracles as verifiable process rewards, but those oracles act as task-specific verifiers in controlled environments (Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b;c). In contrast, Lean4AgenticRL derives verifiable rewards across multiple levels under unified formal language framework for general, open-ended agent executions.

sections.title: 4.2 VERIFIABLE AGENT SYSTEMS
sections.content: As agentic systems mature and are increasingly deployed in high-stakes, long-horizon tasks, growing line of work aims to formally model and verify agent behaviors. Some frameworks provide type-based linter for the agent workflow that is embedded in agent languages (Chase, 2022; Wang et al., 2026a), while others verify tool calls and their execution results (Miculicich et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b; Doshi et al., 2026). More recently, Lean4Agent (Wang et al., 2026b) formalizes agent behavior from workflow to execution in Lean, but it relies on predefined, fixed workflow settings. In contrast to theorem proving (Wang et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025) and code verification (Li et al., 2026), where formal verifiers routinely supply training signals, these agent verifications serve only as runtime checks or post-hoc audits.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: This paper presents Lean4AgenticRL, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards under unified framework based on Lean4, an expressive dependenttype formal language, for open-ended agentic RL. Its problem-specific workflow agent system balances the agents inherent capability with execution controllability. Lean4AgenticRL proposes the workflow formalization methods that extend agent verification beyond fixed workflows to general harnesses. Built on this foundation, Lean4AgenticRL unifies high-level outcome rewards (α), midlevel workflow-stage rewards (β), and low-level toolcall rewards (γ). It also proposes the workflowstage-normalized GRPO algorithm, which aims to resolve the grouping problem in agentic RL. We train the LAR-9B/27B models using Lean4AgenticRL. Extensive experiments on SWE-BenchVerified, TerminalBench-2.0, and 2.1 indicate that they outperform their base models by an average of 9.89% and the second-best model we know on those domains by 5.07%. To the best of our knowledge, LAR-9B/27B achieves the best results among models with comparable size. More

sections.title: A LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Despite the strong results achieved by Lean4AgenticRL, our framework still has some limitations. Firstly, Lean4AgenticRLs verifiability still relies on explicitly bounding agent behavior externally; it does not open the black box of LLMs internal computation to achieve thorough and transparent verification. Secondly, the scope of this work is limited to designing better rewards for agentic RL, without integrating the verification into the harness system at runtime. Finally, Lean4AgenticRL primarily focuses on traditional agentic tasks, such as SWE or general terminal usage, without incorporating visual signals into the RL process.

sections.title: B TERM DEFINITIONS
sections.content: Since the verifiable agent framework through dependent-type language like Lean is new domain that may not be widely known by the community, we present the definition of the terms in this section: 1. Lean 4: Lean 4 is functional programming language and interactive theorem prover based on dependent type theory, whose trusted kernel mechanically checks the correctness of programs and proofs; in Lean4AgenticRL, leveraging the foundation library established in Lean4Agent 2.3.1, we use it as the shared formal foundation for building formal representations for workflows and unifying the multi-level reward signals. 2. Dependent type language: dependent type language, such as Lean, allows types to depend on values, so that single language can express both programs and precise mathematical statements about them, and, under the Curry-Howard correspondence (Sørensen & Urzyczyn, 2006), verifying proof reduces to type-checking term against the type of the statement it proves. 3. Agent workflow: structured plan for solving task, represented as directed graph = V, whose nodes are workflow stages and whose edges specify the allowed transitions between them, including sequential, branching, and loop-back transitions. In Lean4AgenticRL, we also refer to the natural-language PSWF, which carries this structure implicitly, as workflow. 4. Workflow stage: node vi of the workflow graph that represents sub-goal of the task (e.g., reproducing the issue or verifying the fix) is called workflow stage. 5. Agent step: single reasoning-action cycle of the agent, consisting of its reasoning, the toolcalls, and the observation of results, which serves as the atomic unit of trajectory and the granularity at which the γ rewards are assigned. Typically, workflow stage consists of sequence of agent steps. 6. Semantic predicates for agent: Following Lean4Agent Wang et al. (2026b), it is atomic decidable typed functions on the agents execution state and trajectory evidence that describe atomic properties of agent behavior. The property can be verified by Lean or Python code when it is directly decidable, and by an evidence-grounded LLM judge when semantic interpretation is required. 7. Pre-/post-conditions: Functions of predicates attached to each workflow stage vi, where specifies what must hold when the agent enters the stage and the specifies what the stage must establish upon exit, analogous to the pre-condition ρ(pre) post-condition ρ(post) Hoare triple {ρ(pre) i } vi {ρ(post) }. sections.title: D ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: D.1 APPLYING LEAN4AGENTICRL TRAINING TO ADDITIONAL MODELS To demonstrate the effectiveness of Lean4AgenticRL, besides Qwen-3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen-3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026c), we also apply the training method to Qwen-3.627B (Qwen Team, 2026b) for 80 steps and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-304B (Xu et al., 2026) for 40 steps using TMax (Ivison et al., 2026) dataset following the exact same training recipes. For Qwen-3.6-27B base model, we evaluate the results using SWE-Bench-Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and TerminalBench-2.0 (Team, 2025c). The base models performance is 70.0% and 45.6%, respectively, while the trained model yields 74.0% and 53.6% on the results. This indicates an improvement of 4.0% on the SWE task and 8.0% on the terminal-usage task. For DeepSeek-V4Flash-0731-304B, the base model achieves 67.3% on TerminalBench-2.1, while our trained model achieves 72.9%, representing 5.6% improvement. These results indicate that the effectiveness of the Lean4AgenticRL training methods is consistent across model size, model family, and posttraining variants. It further demonstrates the potential of further scaling the Lean4AgenticRL process reward to frontier models in significantly larger sizes. D.2 FAITHFULNESS OF WORKFLOW ANNOTATION In this section, we evaluate the faithfulness of our LLM-based annotations during Lean4AgenticRL. In particular, we have the following three main parts of LLM-as-judge annotation in our framework: Predicate annotation faithfulness: In this type of faithfulness, we evaluate whether the generated workflow in our problem-specific workflow (PSWF) stage has the correct workflow annotation. In particular, we evaluate whether it annotates correct preand postconditions using the correct predicate. The annotation fails in this step if it misses some important predicates. For example, if the acceptance criteria predicate required by the PSWF is missing from the postcondition of the corresponding workflow stage, the annotation is counted as failure. Workflow segmentation faithfulness: This type of faithfulness mainly verifies whether our segmentation process faithfully segmented the execution tool calls into the corresponding general workflow steps. The annotation fails at this step if the segmentation of tool calls spans significantly different workflow steps. For example, if one tool call in SWE agents is writing patches to fix the program, but it is classified as the write test workflow stage, then it is failure. Trajectory verification faithfulness: It mainly covers the faithfulness of the process for our actual annotation of β rewards with the trajectory. One annotation is counted as

sections.content: The results show that the overall failure rate in our evaluation is below 10%, which is relatively low when compared with previous efforts in formal reasoning LLM training (Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025) When taking closer look at the detailed results, the failure cases show that most failures in predicate annotation occur in LLM-as-judge predicates, mainly due to ambiguity in the natural-language criteria relative to the workflow requirements. For workflow segmentation, most errors stem from ambiguity in segmentation. Due to the shared context across workflow stages and the relatively ambiguous indicators for each stage, the failure most commonly occurs in ambiguous cutting-point steps, such as the final verification of the last step, which can also be interpreted as form of situation exploration for the next step. For trajectory verification, the most common failure pattern is chunked context length of 16,384 tokens fed into the LLM judge, which, in some cases, results in context length overflow, causing the LLM judge to make judgments based on an incomplete context and leading to the failure. From the outstanding empirical results shown in Table 1 and the relatively steady increase in Figure 2, there is no significant effect on training stability and performance at this error rate. similar pattern was also observed on previous research on auto-formalization (Wang et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025). To further examine the LLM-based faithfulness validators results, we sampled 60 examples per annotation type, for total of 180 faithfulness annotations. Among them, only one annotation in Predicate Annotation is judged as having an error. In particular, it misclassifies one predicate coreCheckPatterns = "test", which is the checker for normalized bash commands. The LLM annotator treated "test" as test-time-only at the verification level, whereas in practice it is used to test the program in execution. Furthermore, providing this additional context to the annotator does not change its judgment of the predicate annotation, which the authors have subsequently verified to be correct. Thus, we conclude that our evaluation method for the three types of faithfulness of LLM-based workflow annotation is reliable enough to support the conclusions we draw from it. COMPARISON BETWEEN DEPENDENT-TYPE WITH OTHER FORMAL

sections.title: LANGUAGES
sections.content: In this section, we compare the dependent-type language we apply in the Lean4Agent and the Lean4AgenticRL framework with other commonly used formal languages for the specification and verification of agent behaviors. Firstly, dependent-type languages like Lean offer greater expressiveness for uniformly modeling and verifying the agent workflows and trajectories. Other formal languages, such as propositional temporal logics like LTL, reason over sequence of atomic propositions, which means they cannot describe structured data such as nested tool-call arguments or JSON schemas, cannot relate values across different states, and are limited to regular properties. Although it can express counting constraints over loops, more complicated cases, such as every edit being matched by later test run, fall outside the logic. Another commonly applied formal language is the Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) language, such as Z3 (De Moura & Bjørner, 2008). Although SMT solvers support recursive algebraic datatypes and recursive function definitions, their decision

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: procedures are generally unable to prove the properties of self-referential definitions, since doing so requires induction, and some of the loop properties must be handled through induction. In contrast, dependent type formal languages provide inductive types for recursive structures such as nested JSON and workflow graphs, support induction to reason properties about loops and selfreferential definitions, and value-dependent types that allow stages preand post-conditions to be stated directly over the concrete data it consumes and produces, which is vital for self-verification behavior in agent executions. Furthermore, dependent type formal language also inherits the resolution of Russells paradox (Kneale, 1971) through higher-order statements that quantify over predicates and workflows while preventing the self-pointing constructions that render naive set theory inconsistent, whereas LTL and first-order SMT solver languages avoid such paradoxes only by being too weak to express higher-order statements at all. Moreover, temporal formulas and SMT-decidable fragments can be embedded as definitions within Lean, thus single dependent-type formal language can host all of these formalisms while relying on small trusted kernel to verify their results. These advantages are why we chose to use Lean as uniform backbone for formalizing agent behaviors and providing multi-level rewards for agentic RL. DISCUSSION OF FORMAL BOUNDARY FOR LEAN4AGENTICRL Since Lean4AgenticRL still applies LLM-as-judge in many places of the framework, we discuss the boundary between formal verification and informal model behavior in this section. Due to the black-box nature of LLM policy, we are unable to directly verify the interior generation process for the agents. Instead, following Lean4Agent (Wang et al., 2026b), we aim to bound the agents behavior at each workflow stage by formulating preand post-conditions using the semantic predicate system. In particular, the formal boundary of the system is established after the problem-specific workflow has been formalized as Lean code, the execution trajectory has been segmented into workflow stages, and the annotation for LLM-as-judge predicates in the trajectory has been completed. These three steps are performed by LLMs and are unable to be formally guaranteed. Within the boundary, the Lean formulates the atomic predicates into complex expression for modeling agent behaviors. Thus, the major source of informality in our system comes from errors in the LLM-asjudge annotation steps, which is detailed in Appendix D.2. We apply this set of formal boundaries to balance the expressiveness and formal guarantees of our reward system, with informality limited to the workflow formalization and the predicate judgment process. This provides more fine-grained control than simple rule-based LLM-as-judge verification and verifies more properties than traditional pure formal methods.

sections.title: G BENCHMARK AND TASK DETAILS
sections.content: SWE-Bench-Verified contains 500 human-verified issues drawn from 12 widely used Python repositories on GitHub. Given an issue description and containerized repository, the agent must produce Git patch that resolves the issue, and its correctness is determined by repository-level test cases. In contrast, TerminalBench-2.0/2.1 comprises 89 challenging terminal-based tasks spanning SWE, system administration, security, scientific computing, and other general domains. The agent completes each task from its natural-language descriptions by executing commands in the container, and success is assessed by task-specific tests of the final container state. Following common practice, we report mean@3 on SWE-Bench-Verified and mean@5 on both TerminalBench versions, all under randomized seeds. We checked all three evaluation sets against our training data and found no overlap. LLM-BASED ANNOTATION DETAILS H.1 PROBLEM SPECIFIC WORKFLOW FORMALIZATION This section provides detailed explanation of how we formalize our problem-specific workflow as Lean code and verify it for Section 2.3.1. We use one of several frontier models (DeepSeek-V4Pro, Claude-Opus-4.6/4.8, GLM-5.2, and Kimi-K3), depending on availability, with Claude-code to transform the SWE problem-specific workflow (PSWF) WS and its corresponding task statements

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: into static semantic verification schema in the Lean4Agent (Wang et al., 2026b) framework. The prompt for the formalization process is demonstrated in Figure 3. We first construct the workflow schema, graph whose nodes represent workflow stages and whose edges specify transitions, including retries and branches. Subsequently, we annotate the formal semantic representations by specifying the preand post-conditions for each stage, which specify the facts required before and after execution. It is supported by our enhanced predicate system, which is enriched in predicates in the SWE task and further extended to terminal-usage tasks. The predicate here represents the atomic properties for agent behaviors. In particular, the predicates represent variable-level properties of explicit variables in the workflows, information-level components that model the implicit information flowing in the process, and workflow-level predicates that model the high-level goals of the workflows. The transformation of the PSWF into Lean4Agent verifiable form enables verification of internal consistency and lays the foundation for granting rewards in subsequent stages. H.2 WORKFLOW STAGE SEGMENTATION This section details the process of our workflow segmentation. Its inputs are the PSWF, the formalized workflow, and the execution trajectory. The trajectory is sequence of agent steps that include reasoning, tool calls, and their results. The agent step has no direct information about which workflow stage it belongs to. In this stage, we segment the trajectory into different stages. The details of the segmentation prompt are presented in Figure 4.

sections.title: I REWARD ANNOTATION DETAILS
sections.content: I.1 β REWARD ANNOTATION This section provides details of the method we used to annotate the β reward. In particular, following Lean4Agents design, the β rewards determine whether the required postconditions are established by the stages agent executions. For some predicates, we can verify them directly using Lean or Python code, while others may require LLM-as-judge verification. In particular, the latter handles properties that cannot be faithfully specified by programs. All the LLM judgments must be supported by observed evidence. The detailed annotation procedure is presented in Figure 5. I.2 γ REWARD ANNOTATION In this section, we introduce the symbolic rules we judge for γ rewards following Section 2.3.3. We set the γ reward as negative-only guard over each agent step. The detailed rules are as follows: 1. Consecutive repetition: This rule penalizes the third repeated back-to-back run of the same normalized bash command. 2. No-operation commands: It penalizes the command chains consisting of no-operations or delays such as exit, exit 0, true or numeric sleep x. 3. Constant shell output: It penalizes constant-only echo, printf, or print-only cat + constant string chains that neither inspect nor modify the task state. 4. General pure-print script: It penalizes the Python or other form of code snippets whose syntax tree contains only literal-valued print calls and no state-dependent executions. 5. Intermediate no-action: It penalizes the non-final agent step with no executable bash or tool actions to prevent the agent from inflating the step count with reasoning-only turns. 6. No-progress re-execution: It penalizes re-running the same bash command within workflow stage with no environment-modifying tool calls. During training, fast Lean + Python code evaluates the above rules on the trajectory and automatically passes them to the reward server for uniform reward assignment. We use Python tools to parse the initial string into syntax trees, and we represent and verify its properties through predicates in Lean. In particular, we penalize only the steps, without rewarding the agent in γ, to avoid the reward itself becoming the source of hacking. In general, this set of rules can largely prevent the agent from hacking the rewards by inflating the number of steps the agent takes. Combined with the empirical study in Section 3.5.2, we conclude that the method relatively is effective in our experiment settings.

sections.content: J.1 OVERALL ANALYSIS OF THE CASE This section introduces the details for our case study in Section 3.6. We aim to study the training process in detail by analyzing the dynamics of evaluating intermediate checkpoints to elucidate the mechanism. Note that all evaluations are performed post-hoc and are not used to select the best model checkpoint. Such demonstration intends to illustrate the performance of our training and explain why it works by presenting case. In particular, we select the evaluation results of regex-chess for the model checkpoints at the 0-th (base model), 40-th, 80-th, and final 120-th steps, formalizing the PSWF, segmenting the execution-phase trajectory, and annotating the corresponding β rewards. And the model can finally resolve that problem as the process reward steadily grows. This trend indicates that Lean4AgenticRL has the potential to enable the model to acquire capabilities it originally lacks, which has proven to be an important topic in RLVR (Chen et al., 2026). J.2 DETAILED CASE This section presents the abridged execution-phase trajectories of the four checkpoints in Figures 6, 7, 8, and 9; each segmented into PSWF stages with the corresponding β rewards. The base model (Figure 6) builds correct FEN codec and size-valid re.json, and both stages receive β = +1. However, malformed lookahead in its move-rule builder means no move rule ever fires, so the move-rule, output-field, and final verification stages receive β = 1. At step 40 (Figure 7), the model builds move generator that covers castling and en passant, and four of its seven stages earn β = +1. Its remaining failures come from king-safety filter whose knight and pawn offsets are off by one, and from rule tail that does not accept the castling field. At step 80 (Figure 8), the legality filter handles knight checks and pins, queen promotion is tested, and the positions that broke step 40 now pass, which raises the verifier result to 2/4 tests and gives β = +1 on five of six stages. Both remaining failures stem from castling out of check, which the castling guard misses because the PSWF item only requires that the path be empty and the rights be present. At step 120 (Figure 9), the model correctly rejects castling out of check, every stage earns β = +1, and all four tests pass. Taken together, α stays at 1 for the first three checkpoints, while β gives increasingly fine-grained credit for the stages each attempt actually establishes. This provides learning signal before the task is solved, which benefits the learning process.
